title: Getting ready
hook: Friday is for cooking, cleaning and washing, as if a guest were coming

segments.voice: Yesterday, holy time: the first thing called holy was a day. Your line was a palace in time. That ends a week that ran from manna and Jethro to the mountain, the calf, the mishkan and Shabbat.

One hour before guests arrive, the vacuum comes out. Someone shoves mail into a drawer. The good towels go in the bathroom. Somebody's in the shower, somebody's stirring a pot, and the house smells like onions and soap. It's chaos, and it's also a kind of love. In homes that keep Shabbat, that's Friday afternoon, week after week. Someone important is coming at sundown, and the someone is a day.
screen: `AN HOUR BEFORE THE GUESTS.` → `ONIONS AND SOAP.` → `THE GUEST IS A DAY.`

segments.voice: Erev means evening, or eve. Erev Shabbat is Friday, especially Friday afternoon. The roots go back to the manna. On the sixth day, the Torah says, the people gathered twice as much and prepared what they brought in, so there'd be food on the seventh. Getting ready is built into the very first Shabbat. The Talmud tells how the great rabbis spent Friday, and they weren't too important for chores. One singed the head of an animal for cooking. Another salted a fish. Another cut beets; another carried loads in and out of the house. They did it themselves, on purpose, because honoring Shabbat with your own hands was part of it. And as the sun went down, one sage would wrap himself in his cloak, stand, and say: come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the queen. Another would say: come in, O bride. Centuries later, a Friday night song welcoming the Sabbath bride grew from those words. So in many homes, Friday's list goes something like this: cook the meals, because Shabbat has no cooking; clean; set the table with a white cloth; bathe; put on something nice; turn off whatever needs turning off. Some people get ready for hours. Some just do one thing. Either way, it's the idea behind any dinner party. When a guest you love is coming, you don't wait until they're at the door to get ready.
screen: `EREV: THE EVE.` · `TWICE AS MUCH ON THE SIXTH DAY.` · `THE RABBIS DID THEIR OWN CHORES.` · `GO OUT TO GREET THE QUEEN.` · then, large: `GET READY FOR A GUEST.`

segments.voice: Picture the room you'll be in on Friday evening, and find one surface in it: a table, a counter, a nightstand, even the home screen of your phone. Picture it clear, with something small and good placed on it: a cloth, a candle, a plate, a flower. That surface is where the guest arrives.
Erev Shabbat. The eve of the Sabbath: Friday, when homes cook, clean and wash to greet the day like an honored guest.
Your line: get ready for a guest. The chores are part of the welcome. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In many Jewish homes, Friday is spent cooking the Shabbat meals in advance, cleaning, setting a festive table, bathing and dressing up before candle lighting at sundown.
